rawContent:
This is a key point where we differ from mainstream sw eng practices, and I'm aware of this. The problem is exponential blowup.

Say you have a 100 line function register_user, but you have to use different logic for men.

Now you can either copy and paste the function and make register_male_user and register_female_user. You now have 2 100 line functions. Easier to parallelize, easier to fix bugs in, easier to test, etc...and this is why it's mainstream practice.

But now you have to add Canadian users. register_male_us_user, register_male_canada_user, register_female_us_user, register_female_canada_user.

And now you have to handle if they have a dog.
register_male_us_user, register_male_us_user_with_dog, register_female_us_user, register_female_us_user_with_dog, register_male_canada_user, register_male_canada_user_with_dog, register_female_canada_user, register_female_canada_user_with_dog.

This is what more large company codebases look like. Dogshit.

Yes, you need a 130 IQ to touch the 140 line register_user function that handles all, vs a 110 IQ to handle the 8 100 line functions.

But it's a bad tradeoff. You'll get the same bug report 4 times if there's a bug in canada users, but it'll only be fixed in the without dog variants and now we have a new ticket for canadians with dogs 3 months later.

Just do it right. Write one function and test it properly.

rawContent:
Now, the counter to "transformer ASIC" garbage, and why tiny corp targets training.

Transformer inference is simple. The tradeoffs are super well understood, and NVIDIA is very close to optimal. They do have large margins, but even AMD and Intel will get their act together for transformer inference and the margins will lower. For this specific application, you can just write hacks until it works.

However, transformer inference is not the future. Future systems will be lifelong learners. There will be tons of RL (data depends on weights) training. Architectures will continue to improve.

Once you are out of the well trodden, you are in bitter lesson land. Nobody to hand-tune that code, you better be able to search. The magic of tinygrad is not targeting one application, but rather building an OS/compiler that will someday be capable of recursive self improvement.

rawContent:
Thanks for doing it! I don't like this style, I find this takes a lot longer to understand in total, and misses a key point of tinygrad.

Most software projects try to isolate complexity, which is what this refactor attempts to do. This allows large teams to work on them, which is good. But this leads to either tons of repeated code or many layers of abstraction.

Both of these make a project very hard to change, and therefore the project stagnates at a certain point. The complexity in the project increases to a point that it's no longer possible to make forward progress.

tinygrad is making a different bet. Deep learning is simple if only we could get the abstractions perfect. Code velocity (like velocity of money) is a plus, not a minus.

Any LLM can unpack the former into the latter. Now, try to get an LLM to go the other way. (if you succeed at this, what parts of tinygrad can we make shorter?)

GPU tradeoff series: 𝘁𝗶𝗻𝘆𝗯𝗼𝘅 mini-series (ep. 1) 🔥

tinybox (green) is a rig with 6x4090, providing a total of 144GB GPU memory—enough to train the largest GPT-2 (1.5B).

I focus on 2 benchmarks: scalability with # GPUs, and its perf against an H100, both cost ~$25,000.

- Setup
For these benchmarks, I used llm.c to train GPT-2 (1.5B). I used the max batch size that can fit into each GPU (4090 and H100).

- Scalability
The scalability of tinybox is nearly linear, as shown by the graph.
> 1x4090: 11,888 tokens/s

rawContent:
There's a world in which tinygrad becomes the new dominant operating system.

At @comma_ai, we developed a proper successor to ROS. openpilot has serialization (with capnp) and IPC (with zmq + a custom zero copy msgq). It uses a constellation of processes to coordinate to drive a car.

However, the main reason they are separate processes is for scheduling and multicore. Most of them can be rewritten in tinygrad, and can exist in a single process.

From the users perspective, tinygrad is a single thread. Though on the backend, it's a graph compiler, capable of scheduling parallel things in parallel.

Imagine writing a parallel copy program. The common way in Linux is to spawn worker threads and have them pop off a queue. You can do it single threaded with async stuff, but it's very painful. In tinygrad:

a = [Tensor(pathlib.Path(fn)) for fn in in_files]
b = [Tensor(t.shape, f"DISK:{fn}")) for t, fn in zip(a,out_files)]
for x,y in zip(a,b): y.assign(x)
Tensor.realize(*b)

A cleaner expression of operations like that than any modern operating system.

At its core, openpilot transforms images into CAN messages (while keeping around some internal state). Sensors in, actuators out. In one tinygrad graph, scheduled by the backend.

Robots of the future will all run tinygrad.

rawContent:
We are going to.

There's still a ways to go on the software before we know exactly what we are building, but it gets closer every day.

We need:
* Fully parameterized tensor cores to be able to search over that space. Then we can try a ton of different options in emulation and figure out across our model test suite what gets the highest utilization.
* Assembly backends for AMD and NV. We are still using the LLVM based compilers, until we replace this we aren't ready for ISA design yet. Want to use ILP for joint register allocation and instruction selection.
* A lot more thought into mastering the cache hierarchy and warp scheduling on GPUs. Our chip won't have explicit caching, just manually managed SRAM (same as Google TPU). Since everything is statically scheduled we don't have to deal with latency hiding.

Then I think we're pretty close to ready. We'll build an FPGA edition tinybox to develop on and run it all end and end. 

We plan to open source the design and RTL, allow multiple vendors to tape it out and compete on efficiency. Our mission is to commoditize the petaflop. We want to remove moats, not build our own.

rawContent:
Very few people have succeeded at building these machines. There's a few areas of complexity.

1) PCI-E AER errors. It's very hard to get reliable PCI-E extensions. We had to have custom cables made. Most of what you think works doesn't. It works right up until you stress test it.

2) Power supplies. How do you safely use 2 ATX power supplies in a computer? Just connecting them may work...until it doesn't and fries your whole system. They aren't built like server PSUs.

3) The case. If you don't care about this, sure you can use crypto mining cases. But they don't go in racks and aren't enclosed.

4) Quiet reliable cooling. Again, if you don't care about this being nice, use a house fan blowing on your crypto rack. But if you want something that belongs in a living room...

There's no real secrets though, and we encourage people to try to undercut us. Mostly we just want more of these machines to exist, our mission is to "commoditize the petaflop"

rawContent:
Speed is broken down into a few things.

First, there's runtime speed and compile speed. These tests are focused on runtime speed, so based on the code of the kernels generated.

There's a scheduler which determines how the kernels are split and how memory is allocated, this is also not relevant for this test. This test is all about the kernel speed itself.

Are you iterating in a cache-aware way? This is likely why gemm is slow. Check out the OptOps for how to fix that.

Are you generating dumb code because simplification rules are missing? This is likely why cat is slow. Check out the rewrite rules for this.

Are you just passing bad flags to LLVM? Didn't enable the right optimizations? DEBUG=6 will show you the assembly and you can dive in.

'DEBUG=6 LLVM=1 python3 test/test_tiny.py TestTiny.test_plus' is a good place to start seeing the internals. Also, when you are ready, try VIZ=1 (it opens in a web browser)
